narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in traditional practices and cultural heritage. While the source material does not provide explicit information on hairstyles during this specific decade, it offers valuable insights into popular styles and practices that would have been relevant to this era. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of afro-textured hair, was likely gaining popularity as the 1960s approached. Cornrows, a traditional African braiding practice, were also an integral part of Black and African women's hair culture during this time. As protective hairstyles, cornrows allowed women to minimize manipulation and exposure of their hair to environmental elements. The Jheri curl, invented by Jheri Redding in the 1960s but gaining popularity later, was not yet a dominant style in the 1950s. However, the emphasis on natural textures and traditional braiding practices suggests that Black and African women were beginning to reclaim their cultural heritage through their hairstyles.
